rival

/RY-vuhl/ - rhymes with arrival · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Rival means a person or group competing with another for the same goal.

For thirty years the two observatories were friendly rivals, racing to be first to catalogue each new comet.

Example

Elena and Priya met in the ten-and-under heats and have been rivals for the national backstroke title ever since — Elena took it in March, Priya took it back by June. They text after every meet, borrowed each other's coaches once, and will each tell you, without pausing, that the other is the reason she never skips a morning swim.

Rival is the exact word because it names someone competing for the same prize — and nothing more. No ill will is required: the title has room for one name, so they contend for it, and the contest sharpens them both. When hatred does creep into a rivalry, English reaches for stronger words; rival itself stays clean.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

contender: A contender is anyone with a proven, real shot at the prize — the rankings, the record, and the oddsmakers all say so. The word measures chances, not relationships. A rival is the particular opponent you measure yourself against, whatever the odds say about either of you.

challenger: A challenger is defined by the draw, not by history: whoever fights through to face the current holder is the challenger, even a total stranger. A rival is built over time — repeated meetings, traded titles, a name you know. Every rivalry began with a challenger; most challengers never become rivals.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

teammate: on your side of the bracket, win or lose

ally: joined to your cause

Where it sits · how personal the contest becomes

competitor → rival → archrival

competitor vs. rival: A competitor is anyone in the bracket; a rival is the one whose results you check first.

archrival vs. rival: Archrival goes past rival — the one opposite number whose name defines the whole contest.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — riv: stream (Latin rivus)

Suffix — -al: one connected with

Put it together: Riv- (stream — Latin rivus) + -al (one connected with) = one who shares your stream. Latin rivalis named the neighbor drawing water from the same brook — the original contest over something only one could keep. Every rivalry since has held the shape: two parties, one stream, not enough for both.

Use the root in a new word: derive: To derive — literally to draw water off a stream — is what you do when you draw one thing from another's source.

Word Building

Word Choice

neutral

Rival is competition's word, not hatred's: two parties, one prize, and often real respect. That's the line between rival and this unit's adversary, who is set against you in genuine conflict. A rival can become an adversary when the contest turns to combat — but a good rivalry, like the swimmers', never needs to.
